items.title: 'Null and void:' Egypt condemns Turkey-Libya maritime deal, reaffirms pact with Greece
items.summary_raw:
'Null and void:' Egypt condemns Turkey-Libya maritime deal, reaffirms pact with Greece

Egypt has declared a contentious maritime deal sealed by Turkey and eastern Libya as “null and void, absolutely”, reaffirming its commitment to an agreement it sealed with Greece.

Egypt’s foreign ministry on Wednesday “reiterated that the memorandum is null and void, carries no legal effect, and that its ratification by the Libyan House of Representatives entails no legal consequences whatsoever for Egypt”, according to a statement.

Egypt’s statement marks a show of support for Greece, a longtime partner in the Eastern Mediterranean, and underscores Cairo’s own reservations about the Turkish agreement, which directly contradicts one it reached with Athens.

items.title: Kaja Kallas Tells Hakan Fidan Turkish-Libyan Memorandum Violates Sovereign Rights of Third Countries
items.summary_raw:
BRUSSELS – The Libyan Parliament’s ratification of the illegal Turkish-Libyan memorandum was at the center of talks held Wednesday between EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan. According to Kallas’ statement, the EU’s top diplomat raised the issue with Fidan, stressing that the Turkey-Libya Memorandum of Understanding on maritime zones violates the sovereign rights of third countries. Kallas’ intervention came just hours after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa sent Ankara a strong message in support of Greece over the Turkish-Libyan memorandum ratified by the Libyan Parliament. Both leaders emphatically stressed that the memorandum is incompatible with international law and is null and void.

The post Kaja Kallas Tells Hakan Fidan Turkish-Libyan Memorandum Violates Sovereign Rights of Third Countries appeared first on The National Herald.</

items.title: UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
items.summary_raw:
Decision was widely expected after lobbying by Shell but will dismay environmental campaigners

  • What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?

  • UK politics live – latest updates

  • Business live – latest updates

The UK government has approved the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, a widely expected move that will nonetheless dismay environmental campaigners and a number of Labour MPs.

While Labour’s 2024 election manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, the companies behind Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project, which is being decided on separately, have sought environmental approval for existing licences.

items.title: The Financial Times reports that the Israeli military prepared a strike campaign on Iran for October 10 that would have targeted energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and "reg…
items.summary_raw: The Financial Times reports that the Israeli military prepared a strike campaign on Iran for October 10 that would have targeted energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and "regime targets", but cancelled it due to Trump's opposition to resuming strikes before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.   This strike campaign had reportedly been intended to surpass the intensity of the initial joint US-Israeli strikes in February and March. It remains unclear if the U.S. would have taken part in the operation directly.   FT reports that the goal of such an operation would have been to force Iran to agree to American terms surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's nuclear programme, in order to fully end the war.   On Monday, U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth travelled to Israel to meet with Benjamin Netanyahu and other senior Israeli officials. FT reports that Israeli officials presented an "updated target bank" to Hegseth compiled based on new intelligence, including civilian infrastructure targets that had not previously been hit.

The small glacier, on a mountain 8 miles (15km) outside the Norwegian village of Longyearbyen, is a popular summer hike for tourists who come here seeking the Arctic experience.

items.title: Libya Approves Controversial Turkey Maritime Deal, Drawing Objections From Greece, Cyprus and EU
items.summary_raw:
CAIRO (AP) — Libya’s parliament unanimously approved a contested maritime agreement with Turkey on Tuesday, reversing years of opposition and reviving a dispute with Egypt, Greece and Cyprus over rights in the eastern Mediterranean. The House of Representatives, the eastern-based parliament aligned with military commander Khalifa Hifter, voted to adopt the memorandum of understanding signed in 2019 by Turkey and Libya’s then-government in Tripoli, the Government of National Accord. Greece’s Foreign Ministry rejected the vote, saying in a statement that it “does not alter the illegal, invalid and groundless nature of the memorandum.” The ministry said Turkey and Libya do not have opposite or adjacent coasts that could provide a legal basis for delimiting maritime zones. It said the agreement disregards the rights of Greek islands, which lie between the Turkish and Libyan coasts.

The post Libya Approves Controversial Turkey Maritime Deal, Drawing Objections From Greece, Cyprus and EU appeared first on The National Hera

The Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead on Wednesday, signalling Andy Burnham’s commitment to the North Sea fossil fuel industry and threatening to trigger a row with climate campaigners and Labour MPs.

items.summary_raw: BIG: Libya's eastern-based House of Representatives voted to approve the 2019 maritime agreement with Türkiye and reverse its 2020 boycott of Ankara.   The deal, signed by President Erdogan and then-Tripoli government head Fayez al-Sarraj, defines maritime zones in the Eastern Mediterranean.  The eastern parliament, aligned with Khalifa Haftar, had previously declared it null and void.   The shift follows the election earlier this month of a new speaker who once chaired a Libyan-Turkish friendship committee, and growing Turkish outreach to eastern Libya.   The approval could clear the way for expanded Turkish offshore exploration in Libyan waters.

items.title: Do not be distracted by global crises. Nature cannot wait for a better year – we must act now | Steven Guilbeault
items.summary_raw:
In 2022, I helped push through the international agreement to protect biodiversity. Wars and economic pressures can make nature seem like a ‘nice-to-have’. But it is a critical asset, and Cop17 must deliver real action

When I was five, property developers came to cut down the woods behind my home in La Tuque, Quebec. My mother encouraged me to climb one of the trees in protest, then told the developers, straight-faced, that there was nothing she could do when they asked her to get me down. A few days later, the tree was cut down anyway.

I thought about that tree in the early hours of a freezing Montreal morning in December 2022, as the gavel came down on a global agreement between nearly 200 countries to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030. I thought about how important nature is for our health, our food security and our economies, but also how much passion there is around protecting it, and how it has the power to inspire people all around the world.

items.title: ‘Crucial opportunity to act’ as study finds most of Europe’s wild bee species in decline
items.summary_raw:
As Cop17 kicks off, records since 1921 show more bee species declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alps

Most of Europe’s wild bee species and about half of its hover fly species have declined over the last century, a study has found, as a UN biodiversity summit begins in Armenia.

Records since 1921 show more bee species are declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alpine region. The richness of bee and hover fly species suffered a persistent drop in the Atlantic and Continental regions, the study found, though trends in other regions were mixed or even positive.

items.title: Capsizings Cause the Deaths of 12 Migrants off Greek Islands
items.summary_raw:
ATHENS, Greece (AP) — A dozen migrants died in separate speedboat capsizings off the Greek islands of Lesbos and Samos, Greece's coast guard said Monday. An infant was among the dead. Six people died when a speedboat ferrying Syrian and Palestinian migrants struck the port side of a Greek coast guard vessel with its bow and capsized south of Lesbos late Sunday, a coast guard spokesperson told The Associated Press on customary condition of anonymity. Four men, one woman and an infant were among the dead. Another eight people, including an individual who has been detained as the suspected people smuggler, were rescued.

The post Capsizings Cause the Deaths of 12 Migrants off Greek Islands appeared first on The National Herald.

Some gasped for air in their final moments, desperate for the oxygen that heatwave conditions had depleted in the water. Investigators believe that the die-off was triggered by heavy rainfall that flushed through high concentrations of pollution at a time when wildlife were already struggling.

items.title: Tap water no longer drinkable in Norwegian village as climate-related thawing releases heavy metals
items.summary_raw:
Warning for other Arctic communities as residents told not to use water in Longyearbyen in Svalbard, one of the world’s fastest-warming places

Residents of a remote village in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost.

Longyearbyen, in the archipelago of Svalbard, gets its main drinking water supply from a 1.5 mile-long (2.5km) dammed lake called Isdammen, or “ice pond”. Higher temperatures as a result of the climate crisis have thawed permafrost, leading to newly exposed bedrock leaching metals into the pond.

items.title: Approximate flight routes of the missiles used in tonight's large-scale Russian combined attack on Kyiv Oblast.  The following was launched:  ~8 RM-48U modified S-400 ballistic mis…
items.summary_raw: Approximate flight routes of the missiles used in tonight's large-scale Russian combined attack on Kyiv Oblast.  The following was launched:  ~8 RM-48U modified S-400 ballistic missiles from near Klintsy, Bryansk Oblast.  ~7 Iskander-M ballistic missiles from near Klintsy and Pochep, Bryansk Oblast.  ~6 Iskander-K cruise missiles from near Fatezh, Kursk Oblast.  ~21 missiles in total.  Of these 21 missiles, 3 Iskander-K cruise missiles were shot down. None of the ballistic missiles were intercepted due to Ukraine having effectively run out of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors, although 6 out of 8 of the RM-48U missiles missed their target due to their low accuracy.  The following was struck:  - CHP-4 Combined Heat and Power Plant in eastern Kyiv by ~2 RM-48U S-400s.  - "Western" 330 kV electrical substation west of Kyiv by ~2 Iskander-Ms and ~3 Iskander-Ks.  - Unknown (probably industrial) target in western Kyiv by ~5 Iskander-Ms.  - 6 of the RM-48U missiles seemingly missed their target and fell in areas surrounding the CHP-4 Power Plant in eastern Kyiv.

items.title: Cop17 at a glance: everything you need to know about the UN’s nature summit
items.summary_raw:
This month’s biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, aims to push governments to meet the 23 targets agreed at Cop15 in 2022

This month, nearly every country on Earth will return to the question of how to stem the rapid destruction of the natural world. Humans are driving it, but so far we have not found a way to stop it.

In late 2022, governments reached an ambitious once-in-a-decade deal to better protect nature amid scientific warnings that the planet is going through the largest loss of life since the extinction of the dinosaurs. Now, they are assessing their progress on the targets for the first time.

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned US citizens of Iranian access to nuclear weapons, claiming that gas prices will decrease once Tehran's "regime disappears".

In a video message addressed to Americans, Netanyahu says "if you're worried about today's gas prices, think of what will happen if Iran gets nuclear weapons, something that Donald Trump and I will never allow".

He says that if this happens, then the "threat of that regime disappears, gas prices will go down", adding that it can happy only under Trump's leadership. 

"It's not going to happen with those who want to accommodate and appease these tyrants," he said.

items.title: EPA quietly backtracks on claims US has phased out toxic Pfas compounds
items.summary_raw:
Agency changes wording on website as Texas-based firm continues manufacture of plastic container barriers

The Environmental Protection Agency has quietly backtracked on a claim that the US has phased out two of the most dangerous Pfas compounds – Pfoa and Pfos.

The EPA has found that virtually no level of exposure to either in drinking water is safe, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies Pfoa as “carcinogenic to humans” and Pfos as “possibly carcinogenic”. Still, the EPA is allowing Houston-based Inhance to produce containers from which Pfoa has been found to leach at high levels into the containers’ contents. The company makes up to 200m barriers annually for plastic containers use

San Clemente is one of southern California’s most picture-perfect beach towns – a capital of American surf culture since the 1950s. In two years, 2028 Olympic surfers will compete at Lower Trestles, a world-class surfing beach.

But the town’s longtime cultural and economic driver, its beaches, are now under threat. As pounding waves driven by late-summer storms in the Pacific devour chunks of the California coastline, some of San Clemente’s beaches are growing narrower, the sand increasingly eaten away.

According to local sources on base, Canadian Forces personnel had been conducting exercises over several days when an artillery projectile reportedly struck an active natural gas well on the bombing range, triggering a massive detonation.  The blast is said to have levelled nearby tactical training buildings, with subsequent fires reaching munitions storage and setting off secondary detonations across the range. The ‌captain of the LNG tanker said that a small skiff with seven people onboard approached the vessel when it was 140 nautical miles (259km) southeast of the Yemeni port city of al-Mukalla.

The tanker responded by firing ⁠two warning shots at the skiff, and it then altered its course.

“Vessels are advised to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO, whilst authorities investigate,” the agency said.

items.title: US corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report finds
items.summary_raw:
Environmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation Regulation

US corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth.

Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influence the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in more than 350 meetings, the advocacy group found.

Pakistan's finance minister said on Saturday the country had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices due to the Iran war, but that attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were "worrying" for the country's longer-term economic outlook.

In an interview on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Muhammad Aurangzeb told AFP said the South Asian country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.

"The first-order impact has been negotiated well by Pakistan," he said.

items.summary_raw: OSINTdefender Army Chief of Staff General Randy George warned in late December, two months before the Iran war began, that the Army was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage would last until 2030, according to multiple U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News. The Pentagon says claims of munitions shortages are “false.”  The warning was a risk analysis in the Pentagon’s Global Force Management Allocation Plan for fiscal 2027, which sets where troops and weapons go worldwide, the officials said. They said THAAD and Patriot interceptors would stay strategically low, citing Patriot transfers to Ukraine, munitions used to defend Israel during the 12 Day War and reduced industrial capacity. CBS withheld the exact percentages for security reasons. Gen. George declined to comment.  Officials told CBS the U.S. still holds a significant stock of offensive munitions, such as JDAMs and Small Diameter Bombs, but missile defense interceptors are low. One said even with no further use, restoring the already low December 2025 levels would take until 2030. items.title: Josh Huck Officially Assumes Duties as Chargé d’Affaires ad Interim of the U.S. Diplomatic Mission to Greece
items.summary_raw:
ATHENS - Josh Huck officially assumed duties as Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, of the U.S. Diplomatic Mission to Greece, on Thursday October 15, 2026. A career member of the U.S. Foreign Service with the rank of Minister Counselor, Chargé d’Affaires Huck previously served as Deputy Chief of Mission at the U.S. Embassy in Athens. In his new capacity, he will lead the Mission’s continued efforts to advance U.S. priorities and further strengthen the longstanding strategic partnership between the United States and Greece. The United States remains firmly committed to its close partnership with Greece, including expanding defense and security cooperation, strengthening regional energy security, promoting trade and investment, and advancing shared interests in the Eastern Mediterranean and beyond.

items.title: Iguazu Falls in South America hits record 10 times normal water flow – video
items.summary_raw:
Iguazu Falls, an Unesco world heritage site, has reached a record water flow after heavy rains across the river basin. El Niño weather patterns are said to have driven the water flow to hit 10 times the normal amount. Usually the water flow is 1.5m litres per second, but local government registered a flow of 15m litres of water per second.

items.title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
items.summary_raw:
Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia

Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.

Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.

items.title: US military weighs using 'mother of all bombs' if Trump resumes war
items.summary_raw:
US military weighs using 'mother of all bombs' if Trump resumes war

The US military has developed strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother of all bombs", against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations, CNN reported on Thursday citing US officials familiar with the matter.

The potential deployment of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the conflict, although officials familiar with military planning discussions told CNN questions remain over its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.

Report by Reuters
